"It's like...It's like an invisible monster with no shape, no form, but it's loud and fierce and it never ends"
"Right, okay. I mean, is that...Is that the clearest way you can think of to explain it?"
"I'm trying, I'm sorry"
"No, right, it's okay. So how do we defeat this monster?"
"We can't"
"There must be some way. All monsters have a weakness. Maybe it's love. Maybe...Maybe love is how we defeat this monster together"
"Love makes it worse"

When battling depression, there are very few things to say that will come out right and clear. In response to what they cannot understand, to what they feel is unclear yet bigger than them, to what they cannot deal with; as they're going through the motions of self-blame, guilt, self-loathing, all the "Is it something that I did?", while they're asking all the questions, when they've stopped, and all the in between; as they're sifting through defense mechanisms, everyone else who's stuck around long enough to watch it unfold starts behaving erratically, they develop a thing of their own, they build walls of words and carefully craft eccentricities and sometimes become hurtful in an attempt to generate an effect, a feeling, a thing, anything. They struggle to relate and then they hurt themselves in the process, and then, then they leave. 

There's the long, heavy, silence within and then there's 
 all the chaos without, and in between, a vast, void space that keeps the two apart. And then, there are those who can empathize, validate and relate. Those who save lives. 

The burden of dealing with mental illness is a heavy one to bear for both sufferer and their nearest and dearest. This show has been dubbed a black comedy but quite frankly, it's one of the best representation of coping with mental illness and its effects on loved ones, that the media's been able to produce in a while.

comments.text:
From a weird reverie of dark revelation,
Mr Grubb woke up with a strange sensation.
Slipping out through the crack at the back of the lair,
Trudging out through the muck and the thick misted air,
Where the collywobbles warbled their sinister call
And the dingle-baggles scurried on jittery claws.
His ghostly breath mixing in with the fog;
He plonked himself down on a damp, mossy log.
But then in the sludge,
Just a few feet away,
Mr Grubb saw a plant that was quite out of place;
A single buttercup in a pile of faeces.
Mr Grubb tore it up into a pile of pieces.

Nana Grubb sculpt through the sludge and the dirt
The solitary witness of Mr Grubb’s hurt
She gathered the petals and hid them from sight
The buttercup fragments of Mr Grubb’s plight
So Billy and Bella and dear Mrs Grubb,
Would not know his madness, but only his love

Nana Grubb lugged the damn diary of dreams
To the edge of the crag where the swamp water steamed 
Such odious prose, such horrible sadness
Such terrible proof of Mr Grubb’s madness
So she clenched her claws round the cursed journal
And hurled it down to the pit infernal
That Mr Grubb’s sorrow and fear and pain, would never be heard of or witnessed again
Then a quick gust of wind caught the hem of her dress
And tossed the dear fossil straight over the edge
The pages came free, one by one all in sequence 
And fluttered about like a flock of mad secrets 

From a weird reverie of dark revelation
Mr Grubb woke up with a strange sensation
So he turned to the goblin who knew him the best
And brought her soft hands to the depths of his chest
It would beat through the future, as it beat through the past
But how frightening to ponder, when it’s beating that fast
Mrs Grubb said “Be careful, or your poor heart might pop”
“I know” said her husband
“I don’t want it to stop”
